newsitem.title: USA: FDIC's Helfer wary of bank/company combinations.
newsitem.headline: FDIC's Helfer wary of bank/company combinations.

text.p: Federal Deposit Insurance Corp favors modernizing U.S. financial laws but urges caution on the controversial issue of allowing combinations of financial and commercial firms, the agency's chairman said Thursday.

"Current restrictions on the financial activities of banking organizations are outdated," chairman Ricki Helfer said in prepared testimony for a Congressional hearing. "Their elimination would strengthen banking organizations by helping them to diversify their income sources, and would promote the efficient, competitive evolution of financial markets in the United States."

Such reform, however, "must ensure that the safety and soundness of insured depository institutions and the integrity of the deposit insurance funds and other elements of the safety net will not be compromised," she said in her remarks before the House Banking Committee's financial institutions subcommittee.
Some Congressional proposals would tear down legal barriers not just between banks and other financial sectors, but also allow common ownership of financial and commercial enterprises.
Helfer said easing the broader restrictions "beyond those that are financial in nature should proceed cautiously."
A bill introduced by Rep Marge Roukema, Republican of New Jersey, would allow financial companies to conduct up to 25 percent of their business in commercial activities.
Helfer said that approach "is one option that should be considered."
In modernizing U.S. law, Congress should protect the federal deposit insurance fund but not impose geographic or product-specific limits on banks, Helfer said.

"Atempts to ensure the safety and soundness of insured institutions by limiting market competition ultimately fail," Helfer said in her prepared remarks. "In the long run, geographic constraints and product restrictions do not insulate depository institutions from competitors, who will eventually find ways to enter markets."

Helfer said the FDIC could accept banks conducting new activities either through direct subsidiaries or one step removed through a holding company structure, as long as sufficient safeguards protected the federal insurance fund.

"It is clear that there are advantages and disadvantages to both the bank holding company and the 'bona fide subsidiary' models," Helfer said. "Legislation based on a progressive vision of the evolution of financial services need not mandate a particular structure as long as the insured bank is protected."
But bank reform should maintain safeguards contained in the Federal Reserve Act that place restrictions on transactions between banks and their affiliates, she said.
"Exceptions under these safeguards should be allowed rarely," Helfer said in her prepared testimony.
